title: Fotufilm: an open-source film simulation engine

posts.raw:
Hi everyone. Over the past few months I've been developing Fotufilm, an open-source film simulation engine for photos and videos. It grew out of a personal curiosity and a hobby. Rather than approximating the "film look" through creative 3D LUTs or subjective colour grading, I was trying to see how much of a film's true response can we recreate purely from manufacturer datasheets and physical sensitometry?

The engine currently models 40 film stocks which spans colour negative, b&w, slide, motion-picture and instant film. You can explore it directly in the browser editor here [demo](https://fotufilm.com/demo) (uses WebGPU, WASM), or run it via the Mac app, and plugins for Davinci Resolve and Final Cut Pro.

Source: https://github.com/DhaliwalX/fotufilm-engine.

## How the simulation works

At its core, Fotufilm follows the physical path of light through emulsion exposure, chemical development, and optical printing:

1. **Spectral estimation**: Input images (ideally scene-linear HDR or OpenEXR) are converted into estimated continuous spectral radiance. Because three RGB channels cannot uniquely reconstruct a full continuous spectrum, this initial step is inherently an approximation, but it allows the film's published spectral sensitivity curves to calculate how each emulsion layer actually responds to scene light. High-dynamic-range inputs are especially important here, as clipped highlight values in 8-bit JPEGs lose the overexposure information that drives natural shoulder roll-off and halation.
2. **Emulsion density and layer interactions**: The calculated exposures pass through the film's characteristic curves (D-log H) to determine developed dye density. The model accounts for chemical adjacency effects and inter-layer interactions where development in one layer inhibits or enhances neighbouring dyes.
3. **Physical halation and grain**: Light spreading within the film base causes characteristic highlight blooms (halation), while film grain is synthesized from simulated clump structures. Both grain appearance and halation spread are physically coupled to the selected film format (from Super 8 up to large-format sheet film).
4. **Print media and scanning**: The developed negative density then exposes a simulated print medium, such as Kodak Ektacolor Edge, Endura, or Fuji Crystal Archive paper, or passes through a simulated lab scanner or light box. The choice of paper dramatically shapes the final image, as each print stock carries its own spectral sensitivities, dye absorption spectra, and contrast curves.


## Exploring the profiles

The examples below were rendered from scene-linear EXRs in the OpenEXR sample collection on their github using standard profile defaults (unless noted). For reference, panels marked **Collection preview** show the collection's own tone-mapped JPEGs, which use an entirely separate display rendering.

### Film stocks and color character

Different emulsions reveal distinct personalities across the same scene:

![Collection preview, Gold 200, Portra 400 and Velvia 50 |690x313](upload://qsySdwKBcadfRyEEjFYtYR5GEuC.jpeg)

###### *MtTamWest, GoldenGate, and Kapaa across multiple stocks. The Vision3 250D example is printed onto Kodak Vision 2383 motion-picture release print stock.*

### Physical effects: halation and format-dependent grain

Halation occurs when intense light penetrates the emulsion and reflects off the backing layer:
![halation-pair|690x234](upload://8H9S8YgG3lFUiPz248gk8o77xBY.jpeg)
###### *CineStill 800T halation off and on*

Because film grain consists of physical silver halide crystals and dye clouds, enlarging a smaller negative magnifies the texture:

![grain-gauges|690x193](upload://aPXeKHdGZLqCMunOQgOPcMcdW8R.jpeg)

## A comparison with spektrafilm

I first began building Fotufilm in isolation as a personal experiement to see if I can derive back the original light data from the image/sensor and then model the film chemistry on the basis of datasheets. I discovered spektrafilm only very recently while opening up to publicise my project.

Discovering spektrafilm and the active discussions around it on PIXLS.US was exciting, as it showed a shared community passion for physical, measurement-based simulation rather than empirical LUT fitting. Naturally, I was curious how the two engines' outputs compare when fed identical scene-linear inputs.

### ColorChecker response
To test color behavior, I ran an sRGB color patch target through both engines using Kodak Gold 200 printed on Kodak Ektacolor Edge. For spektrafilm, I generated a 129-cube LUT using its native tooling (spektrafilm profiles are CC BY-SA 4.0, by Andrea Volpato). For Fotufilm, stochastic and optical effects (grain, halation, flare, and local tone mapping) were disabled to isolate the base color transform.

Across the 512 patches, Fotufilm rendered slightly lighter overall, with an average lightness difference of 3.73 L* and a mean colour difference of ΔE₀₀ 6.55.

Samples below
![comparison-mttamwest-gold200-edge|690x260](upload://1zVmjIe7Ntr9lkLIBUNSe8Q7r50.jpeg)



## Looking forward & call for scans

Several areas remain open for improvement, notably refining print illuminant spectra and resolving discrepancies in published ETERNA-CP dye and neutral curves.

If you have access to controlled film scans with documented film stock, exposure, development chemistry, and scanning conditions, or if you spot behavior that conflicts with published sensitometry, I would love to hear from you. Technical feedback, edge-case testing, and discussion are very welcome!

## Technical details

* **Core engine**: Written in Swift with image-processing pipelines implemented in Halide with the help of Claude/Codex.
* **Platform**: MacOS, Web (there is a partly written linux port for the engine using vulkan and cuda). But it should be fairly straightforward as Swift and halide both work well with cross-platform code.
* **Licensing**: Code is licensed under Apache-2.0. Film profiles are licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 (this applies solely to profile definitions, not your rendered photographs or videos).
* **My background & disclosures**: I am a software engineer at Google who has worked on image processing pipelines for the Pixel Camera, this project is not affliated with them. I did this mostly in my free time.

> The figures in this post were generated using rendering code from Fotufilm `93eb85b` .

Hi @DhaliwalX 

Welcome to pixels! Your project looks awesome.

I’m just a user, not a dev. And I use Linux, fyi.

If your goal is a standalone app, then I would think you may be heading in a good general direction. The original spektrafilm is experimental and is written in python, so it’s a bit slow. But wow, the results are great!

Spektrafilm has some momentum with the community here, with the base code adapted for an OFX plug-in for Resolve (fantastic), a rust port I think, integration into the vkdt editor (also wonderful), and a module for darktable is under development and test. There is probably other work I’ve omitted.

My very limited non-expert experience is that there are advantages in having a mature image/video pipeline that feeds into the film emulation. For me, it is easier and more flexible to process images this way, even though perhaps the overall approach deviates from the concept of “pure film emulation.” I would guess, as you suggest, that mapping rgb to full-spectrum input is a part of the challenge.

My selfish perspective as a general user would be to find that efforts like yours somehow gets merged into some of these efforts. Perhaps starting with the upstream python app and also to a compiled stand alone app too.

In any case, I wish you well, whatever direction you go. 🙂

On which is more accurate, I wouldn’t claim that Fotufilm’s is more accurate just from these comparisons. The default model varies density before the final print/viewing conversion, with grain scale tied to the selected film format. It’s still an approximation, and establishing accuracy would need controlled comparisons with real film.

On the “free tier” comment: that’s a leftover from when I was developing Fotufilm privately and was still undecided about whether and how to monetise it. I should have cleaned up that wording. Infact iOS app is still paid. I’d like to make that free too. The AI subscriptions I use for development add up, and I’ve also been gathering film cameras for experiments. Film, processing and scanning will bring their own costs. Fortunately, I have a job, so these expenses have been manageable so far! I’m still figuring out the longer-term balance.
